draft_context.source_title: UK's Online Safety Act has made 'absolutely no difference,' kids say
draft_context.description: Children have told England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, that the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA) "has made absolutely no difference" to their ability to access harmful content online. More than a year after the OSA's key child protection duties took effect, de Souza told MPs and peers that young people had little understanding of the legislation or how it was intended to change their online experiences. De Souza made the comments during the opening evidence session of the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee's inquiry into the OSA's implementation and impact. Central to de Souza's criticism was the legislation's focus on moderating harmful content rather than addressing potentially harmful platform design features. UK politicians had pushed for controls covering such features, either through the OSA or separate legislation, but none has materialized. De Souza said she was "really cross" that there was no hard evidence showing the OSA had meaningfully changed how social media platforms operate. She contrasted that with the US, where legal pressure recently pushed Meta toward significant child safety concessions. Concerns about addictive platform design are not new, but they have returned to prominence following Meta's proposed $18 billion settlement in a US child safety case. Without admitting wrongdoing, Zuckercorp would under the proposed settlement introduce two-hour daily limits for users under 18 on Facebook and Instagram, prompts intended to discourage endless scrolling, and measures addressing use during school hours and at night. The proposal would also let children opt out of algorithmically ranked feeds, directly addressing concerns raised by de Souza and other UK lawmakers. Discussing the proposed Meta settlement, de Souza said the OSA had "not been flexible enough" and had not "kept up with the time." She argued that Ofcom and lawmakers should seek results comparable to those achieved through the US legal system, even if that required the legislation to evolve. 'Furious' with Ofcom De Souza said she planned to exercise her statutory powers to compel Ofcom, the OSA's regulator, to provide copies of the safety risk assessments submitted by technology companies. The commissioner said Ofcom had refused to share the assessments with her, despite her position as "the most senior safeguarding person in this country for children," and had indicated that it would resist disclosure even if she invoked those powers. "One thing I did want to ask this committee was for your assistance in this matter, because I am planning to use my powers," De Souza said. "If we cannot even see the risk assessments that may well have put these [safety] mechanisms into place, or may not have, how on earth can we judge the efficacy of it? "So I'll leave that one with you, but I'm pretty furious about that." The obstacle is section 393(1) of the Communications Act 2003, which restricts Ofcom's disclosure of information obtained through its regulatory functions. Ofcom may disclose such information if the business concerned consents or if one of the statutory gateways in section 393(2) applies. Asked whether compelling tech companies to complete risk assessments was enough to ensure meaningful change or whether further legislation was needed, the Children's Commissioner said "we need a few things," including for Ofcom to "use its teeth." Ofcom has materially upped its presence in the tech regulation landscape during the past year, stepping in on multiple occasions when needed. Perhaps most notably this was at the height of the Grok nudifying furore, but also its sprawling list of investigations into pornography companies allegedly violating age verification requirements. De Souza acknowledged all of this, and the fact that since the introduction of the latest US administration, UK politicians have not given the regulator the "air cover" needed to relentlessly pursue offenders. Nevertheless, she said Ofcom had failed to bare its teeth as forcefully as the current technology landscape demanded and accused it of reacting to harms rather than anticipating them. "If Ofcom is going to be the vehicle to protect our children… we need them to be getting ahead of the harms. And I don't think they have. "So when I talk around the country to children, what's worrying them are things around AI, things around the nudifying apps… there are new harms, and we need Ofcom to be getting ahead of those. I don't think they are." De Souza called on UK politicians "to be really strong and direct" in empowering Ofcom to pursue offending organizations. "But how effective do I think they've been? Not effective enough." The commissioner also criticized Ofcom's child safety codes under the OSA, which she said read more like technical documents for technology companies than protections designed for children. She also called on Ofcom to "use all their powers," impose "some big fines," and act before new harms become entrenched. The Register asked Ofcom to respond. A spokesperson said: "We work closely with the Children's Commissioner and share her objectives to ensure children are safe online. "In December, we published our analysis of risk assessments from the first year of the Online Safety Act being in force, and the improvements we expected to see from platforms. "Our action has resulted in material improvements being made to risk assessments, ensuring that tech companies must implement all measures necessary to address the risks identified on their sites and apps. "We are subject to laws that mean we're restricted in what information we can disclose relating to businesses." ®

I’m no stranger to AI in home security , but Eufy’s approach is unique and has the potential to be particularly advantageous for customers.

draft_context.source_title: Adobe’s Slack integration brings AI content creation to workplace chats
draft_context.description: With the launch of a new integration this week , Adobe is making more than 70 Creative Cloud applications available in Slack, promising to bring generative AI (genAI) document creation closer to team conversations. The Adobe MCP (model context protocol) integration allows Slack users to access, edit, and create new documents from Adobe creative and productivity tools without switching apps. This includes Photoshop, Premiere, InDesign, Lightroom, and others. The integration should help “improve efficiency and speed of content creation,” said Irwin Lazar, principal analyst at Metrigy. “We have consistently found in our research that companies want to use their team collaboration apps, like Slack, as work hubs.” To access the integration, users interact with Slackbot — Slack’s AI “teammate” — via natural language prompts. Adobe outlined several use cases in a blog post Wednesday. It’s possible to turn “project plans and conversations” in Slack into “PDFs, images and videos you can share with your team in Slack,” and turn speadsheet data into a “PDF or visual you can share with your team or client.” Other uses include the ability to edit images such as headshots and event photos in bulk — with controls available to adjust lighting and tone, crop and resize images, and more — as well as to search for Creative Cloud assets from Slack. The editing interface is more limited than in the full Adobe apps, which Adobe said users can switch to when they want “greater creative control” and “pixel-level precision.” The Adobe integration is available to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ customers. Adobe said that most Adobe apps are “currently available for free to users,” though it didn’t confirm whether this is a temporary or long-term pricing structure. The integration includes access to some generative AI features, with daily usage limits, though others, such as generative video, require paid Adobe accounts. Overall, the move is part of a wider effort by Slack to make AI tools available where work conversations occur. That was the idea behind the recent Slack Code launch , for instance; it’s aimed at aiding interaction with AI coding assistants for multiple coworkers around one-off software development tasks such as bug-fixes and feature updates. For Adobe, it’s a continuation of efforts to make its software available in other platforms. The company recently announced ChatGPT integration that lets users create and edit content from the AI assistant. The Adobe integration with Slack allows conversations and work to “move closer together,” said Joe Cicman, principal analyst at Forrester. “Instead of Slack being where requests are discussed and Adobe being where changes are made, the conversation itself can increasingly become part of the creative workflow,” he said. “More broadly, we’re seeing enterprise software move toward bringing capabilities to the worker rather than forcing the worker to move between applications,” he said. Cicman expects that the ability to interact with Adobe tools in Slack will appeal first to “hands-on marketers and content creators who want to prototype ideas quickly or generate variants of existing assets. “More broadly, it appeals to people who have more ideas than they have expertise in Adobe’s professional tools,” he said. “They know what they want to create, but not necessarily how to navigate Photoshop, Premiere, or Illustrator. Conversational interfaces let them express intent instead of mastering the UI.” There are other considerations about an integration that enables users to generate content with greater ease. It could, for example, increase the production of low-effort, AI-created documents within organizations. According to Adobe, the goal of the integration isn’t only to help workers create more content, but to “express their ideas, contribute to the creative process and bring those ideas to life faster. “By making Adobe’s pro-grade tools accessible through conversation, people across teams can more easily explore ideas, build on each other’s thinking and collaborate on how to make the work better,” a spokesperson said. “At the same time, making creation easier only makes human judgment more important. Adobe’s tools can accelerate the creative process, but people still bring the ingenuity, taste and point of view that distinguish great work. “For brands, that human perspective is ultimately what turns content into something that stands out and creates a meaningful connection with an audience.” Easier content generation could require companies to more closely manage an acceleration in AI-generated outputs,” said Cicman. “What’s happening across marketing and creative teams is that prototyping is becoming dramatically faster,” he said. “A marketer with a concept can describe it in Slack, AI can generate several potential executions, and suddenly the organization has many more ideas moving through the pipeline. The challenge is that faster creation creates a pile-up of work that needs to be reviewed, refined, and approved.” A natural outcome from reducing the cost of prototyping, said Cicman, is the emergence of a new operating model for teams. “Historically, designers spent a significant amount of time creating initial concepts from scratch. Increasingly, AI can generate those first drafts,” he said. As a result, a designer’s role “shifts toward refinement, curation, editing, and applying taste. “In that model, the marketer contributes the concept, AI produces the prototypes, and the designer elevates the work from ‘technically generated’ to ‘creatively excellent,’” he said. “The organizations that benefit most won’t be the ones that generate the most content. They’ll be the ones that combine abundant AI-generated prototypes with strong human judgment and creative taste.”

draft_context.source_title: Windows 11 update sends some desktops into an unwanted goth phase
draft_context.description: Microsoft's August update preview has painted some Windows 11 desktops black – and affected users can't simply restore their preferred backgrounds. Microsoft has confirmed reports that the update can prevent personalization settings from loading on Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2. In an unfortunate Rolling Stones tribute, the operating system consequently falls back to its default black background, regardless of the values users enter. In its entry on the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft added: "It is possible other desktop settings may be affected, such as slideshow settings or contrast themes. "On affected devices, attempting to manually restore customized settings does not work. This is because the issue prevents the correct loading of settings, regardless of their value. In this case, a default black background is used instead." In other words, affected users cannot restore their preferred settings and may be stuck with the black background until Microsoft supplies a fix. The Rolling Stones' Paint It Black turned 60 this year and concerns grief and loss – emotions familiar to anyone who has optimistically installed a Windows update only to be greeted by unfortunate results. As for that fix, Microsoft wrote: "We are working on releasing a resolution for this issue in a future Windows update." For some Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2 users, the operating system has entered its goth period. Customers have complained about dark mode support for years, but turning the entire desktop black probably isn't the resolution they had in mind. An update that doesn't arrive loaded with issues would be a start. ®
paragraphs: Microsoft's August update preview has painted some Windows 11 desktops black – and affected users can't simply restore their preferred backgrounds.

Microsoft has confirmed reports that the update can prevent personalization settings from loading on Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2. In an unfortunate Rolling Stones tribute , the operating system consequently falls back to its default black background, regardless of the values users enter.
In its entry on the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft added: "It is possible other desktop settings may be affected, such as slideshow settings or contrast themes.

"On affected devices, attempting to manually restore customized settings does not work. This is because the issue prevents the correct loading of settings, regardless of their value. In this case, a default black background is used instead."
In other words, affected users cannot restore their preferred settings and may be stuck with the black background until Microsoft supplies a fix.

The Rolling Stones' Paint It Black turned 60 this year and concerns grief and loss – emotions familiar to anyone who has optimistically installed a Windows update only to be greeted by unfortunate results.

draft_context.source_title: How ad-free streaming became so much less affordable
draft_context.description: Ad-free streaming used to be one of the biggest benefits of cutting the cable TV cord. Now it’s become a luxury. Inspired by some new research into the growing price gap between ad-supported and ad-free streaming, I decided to calculate how much the cost to avoid commercials has increased over time. Depending on which services you have, you could be paying an extra $42.50 just to skip ads, up 60 percent from a few years ago. Not all hope is lost for affordable ad-free TV, but you might have to get a bit creative to get it. The increasing ad-free tax My impetus for writing this is a new report from Ampere Analysis about the growing gulf in price between ad-free and ad-supported streaming. The study found that globally over the past three years, the ad-free tiers of Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Disney+ have increased by $1.61 on average, versus $1.21 per month with ads. Those results actually understate the problem. When you look at the United States in particular, which includes more streaming services, the ad-free tax becomes even bigger. Let’s say you’re a subscriber to Netflix, Amazon Prime, HBO Max, Disney+, Paramount+, and Peacock. At the end of 2022 (when both Netflix and Disney launched ad-supported tiers), the total cost would have been roughly $44 per month with ads, or $70.50 without ads, for a difference of $26.50. Those same six services now cost roughly $63 per month with ads, or $105.50 per month without ads. While the overall price has increased on both sides, the difference between ad-free and ad-supported plans has jumped by 60 percent, from $26.50 to $42.50 per month. Here’s a closer look at how the price gap has grown over the years: Dec. 2022 (ads / ad-free) Sept. 2026 (ads / ad-free) Ad-free fee increase Netflix (Standard) $6.99 / $15.49 $8.99 / $19.99 +$2.50 Amazon Prime Video $8.99: Ad-free only $8.99 / $13.98 +$4.99 HBO Max $9.99 / $14.99 $10.99 / $18.49 +$2.50 Disney+ $7.99 / $10.99 $11.99 / $18.99 +$4.00 Paramount+ $4.99 / $9.99 $8.99 / $13.99 $0.00 Peacock $4.99 / $9.99 $12.99 / $19.99 +$2.00 Total $43.94 / $70.44 $62.94 / $105.43 +$15.99 Amazon is the biggest offender. At the start of 2024, it started including ads in Prime Video and charged $3 per month to remove them. The ad-free price then jumped to $5 per month last March, with a plan that Amazon now calls “ Prime Video Ultra .” Other companies were more subtle in pushing ads on users. Disney initially indicated that its ad-supported tier would cost less than the ad-free plan . When that plan arrived in late 2022, Disney raised the price of for ad-free streaming and slotted in its new ad-supported plan at the old price. Netflix, meanwhile, phased out its “Basic (Ad-Free)” plan in 2024, making the jump to ad-free streaming more drastic. And Peacock has raised prices so aggressively that even its ad-supported plan costs more than the ad-free version once did. In all cases, the dynamic is the same: As Ampere points out , subscription growth is leveling out in the United States, and streamers are increasingly relying on advertising to boost their revenues. While ad-free streaming becomes more of a luxury, the streamers still need to keep ad-supported prices low so they can bring in new subscribers and scale up their advertising businesses. Ad skipping still remains alive and well in the realm of live TV streaming services such as YouTube TV, Sling TV, and Fubo. Those services include cloud-based DVRs, so you can record live TV and skip the commercials. But as more viewers opt for cheaper standalone streaming services, the streamers are now ushering the DVR toward obsolescence. What you can do about it In some cases, bundling services together may provide price hike relief, even on ad-free tiers. Disney, for instance, has actually shrunk the price gap for its bundle of Disney+ and Hulu. That package cost $10 per month with ads or $20 per month without ads a few years ago. Now it’s $13 per month with ads, but still $20 per month without ads. The bundle of Disney+, Hulu, and HBO Max has also maintained the same $13 per month upcharge for ad-free over the past couple years, even as the overall cost has increased. (It’s $33 per month for all three without ads.) The growing price gap may also create an opportunity for more affordable ad-free services. I keep writing about how YouTube is taking over TV viewing in the United States, and it now has 125 million subscribers on its Premium or Music plans. If you just want to skip ads on YouTube, Premium Lite for $9 per month can look like a pretty good value compared to traditional streaming services. Keep an eye on Roku’s Howdy streaming service as well. At $3 per month with no ads, the catalog is heavy on B-movies and forgotten reruns, but has some hidden gems that remind me of Netflix’s early days . It reportedly topped 1 million subscribers in less than a year, and it continues to grow its catalog with new licensing deals . If you’re up for a more adversarial approach, you can also take ad-skipping into your own hands. I’ve previously written about PlayOn , which records video from ad-supported streaming services and lets you skip the commercials. Using it can be a hassle, as it requires either pay-as-you-go cloud recording credits or a Windows PC to run the recording engine, but the savings can be significant. If you’re willing to watch through a web browser, the Multi Skipper extension will attempt to fast forward through commercials on major streaming services for free. I’ve been using this on my still-experimental living room PC setup with great success, and while relying on a computer for streaming has its own trade-offs, it’s one of the last ways to retain some control in a system that’s increasingly stacked against its viewers. Sign up for Jared’s Cord Cutter Weekly newsletter for more streaming TV advice.
paragraphs: Ad-free streaming used to be one of the biggest benefits of cutting the cable TV cord. Now it’s become a luxury.

Inspired by some new research into the growing price gap between ad-supported and ad-free streaming, I decided to calculate how much the cost to avoid commercials has increased over time. Depending on which services you have, you could be paying an extra $42.50 just to skip ads, up 60 percent from a few years ago.
Not all hope is lost for affordable ad-free TV, but you might have to get a bit creative to get it.

My impetus for writing this is a new report from Ampere Analysis about the growing gulf in price between ad-free and ad-supported streaming. The study found that globally over the past three years, the ad-free tiers of Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Disney+ have increased by $1.61 on average, versus $1.21 per month with ads.
Those results actually understate the problem. When you look at the United States in particular, which includes more streaming services, the ad-free tax becomes even bigger.

draft_context.source_title: How Sonos rebooted itself
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 . Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them. Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it. Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Tom Conrad, you’re the CEO of Sonos. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. As they say, it’s so great to be here. I am just going to say, finally, I have been asking you to be on the show for at least a year, if not before. I think the first time I met you was in the back of a car at CES when you were at Pandora. Sounds right. One hundred years ago. One hundred years ago. We were children. [Laughs] We were little babies. That car was driven by a human driver. That’s how far back it was. That’s right. And then you took a turn through Quibi. You and I talked through that, and now you’re at Sonos. As you know, I’m a huge fan of Sonos. We had your predecessor, Patrick Spence, on the show a bunch of times . Many things have happened, so I just want to start at the very beginning of this. You’re about a year into being the permanent CEO of Sonos. You have a bunch of news to announce. Just tell us what you think Sonos is today. What is your conception of this company? When I came in the door, one of my earliest observations was that the company behaved like it was 100 percent hardware, but we’re really 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. And if you get either one of those even a little bit wrong, the impact is tremendous. So how does that show up really day-to-day? It was about returning the company to the idea that Sonos doesn’t make these individual products, but we really make one thing — we make the Sonos system. It all has to hang together in a cohesive, interesting, and valuable way, or we’re just not doing the work. There’s been a bunch of basic blocking and tackling, of course, both operationally and in the work that we’re doing in the product family. But at the highest level, returning the company to the idea that we are a system for audio in the home has been the highest-level mantra. When you say come into the company, do you mean as a board member or as the CEO? I mean, let’s start the starter pistol in January of 2025, 18 months ago, when I stepped in first as interim CEO and then was lucky enough six months later to be asked to take the job more permanently. The reason I asked that question is that you obviously have two different views of the company in different roles. We did have former CEO Patrick Spence on several occasions, and he said something very similar to me when he first took over — that Sonos was stuck in its ways. It was really focused on very, very slow iterations of hardware. He tried very hard to push the metabolism of the company to be much faster, and he talked about that very openly with me. That led eventually to what I think is a moment of true crisis: the app launch. It was a disaster. The system stopped working. That’s when you came in to right the ship. Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in. So as you describe, I’ve been involved with the company going back almost 20 years. We brought Pandora to Sonos in 2007, I think, and I was able to get to know the company as a partner before I got to know it as a board member. I came onto the board in 2016 right as Patrick became CEO. So from the vantage point of a board member, I got to participate in Patrick’s chapter. I guess the way I would characterize his high-order thinking about the company in those early days was that, as you described, he wanted to turn the company into a product execution machine with an emphasis on hardware products. We call them NPIs, or new product introductions. In the chapter before him, it was sometimes years between new Sonos products. Spence said, “Look, we’re going to make a company that knows how to ship a couple of great new products a year.” And he did that. I mean, the company has reliably shipped a couple of great products, hardware products, every year, for close to a decade now. Sometimes, when you energize an organization around an idea, there are unintended consequences. I think one unintended consequence of that framing was that the company became very focused on the individual products, one at a time. Even as a board member, I received Roam as a portable speaker with a certain amount of battery life, waterproofing, and Bluetooth connectivity. I didn’t really think about it as a member of the Sonos system. Even with the software work that we did, and with every product that we make, there is a tremendous amount of software effort and innovation that goes into them. But even the software that we made was very focused on the individual NPIs. “What can we do in software to differentiate Move 2 from other speakers in that category?” What was hard to do, and what was hard to prioritize in the company, was horizontal slices of software experiences that benefited all of the platform. So, in a way, I think some of that debt accumulated, and the company thought that the antidote was to recreate the app experience. And as you know, we made a bunch of mistakes at that moment. I’m really proud of the fact that I think we’re well beyond that chapter now, but we could have been much more thoughtful about how we qualified that product in the real world. We could have been much more thoughtful about how we rolled it out to customers. We could have, candidly, I think, examined the original impetus in the first place. It was very Sonos-motivated. We wanted to put the app on a modern architecture to make us more nimble. In my chapter at Sonos, I’m really trying to bring it all back to how we can focus on the customer first. I’m so inspired by talking to people on social media and in my inbox, and people in the industry, like you, about how we show up and solve the real problems that are happening in real households. I’m so excited about the things we’re going to talk to you about today because I think they’re really an answer to many of those questions. If you’re a listener, you know I’m familiar with Tom. The man’s on Threads doing customer support every day. And actually, I should not take advantage of this. I hold myself back from asking you for direct customer support all the time. Anytime. The way that you can tell it’s actually me and not our crackerjack social team is that I often will let a Thread die before I should or fail to follow up with someone. So if we were executing perfectly on that, you would know it was fake Tom, but it’s real Tom, and I do it when I can, but sometimes imperfectly. At least it’s not an AI avatar Tom. That’s when we know it’s going to go sideways. [Laughs] That’s right. I know you’re a Decoder fan, so I’m going to make you sit in this for just one more moment because I find all of this to be really fascinating. The app shipped, and the feedback was immediately and intensely negative. Many, many things were broken. Speakers weren’t working at weddings. This is a time of massive crisis. The company goes to resolve it, but then you’re on the board, and it’s clear that there’s going to be a leadership transition, that Patrick needs to go, and we need a new CEO. And then we’re going to make new custom ones out of building blocks that are enabled in lots of different ways. When I asked where the computer is, this is, to me, the big question: where does all this ambient agentic AI actually live? Where does it have control? Is it going to happen locally? Are we sending everything to the cloud? Somewhere in your home, if you’re going to control lights, music, and everything else, there needs to be some logic happening in your home. There are a lot of standards to do that. Some of them are good, some of them are bad. Some of them have names that connect directly to the word fabric, like Thread. Sure. There’s a lot going on here in terms of just the names and schemes of what could happen. Where do you see this view? Who is your competition here? Is it that Apple is going to launch a new HomePod with an AI-enabled Siri, and they already have a HomeKit, which is a pretty well-built and pretty popular smart home platform? Is it, “Well, OpenAI is going to have a hardware device, and maybe their first one’s going to be in the home, and you need to stave that off and make sure people are talking directly to you, and you have the customer relationship”? That seems not only undeveloped, but even the foundations of how you build the products — like Matter and smart home standards — are messy and political in very specific ways. So how do you see the competition, victory, and success there? And then how do you solve just the capability gap that every other company has run into? So one thing that I’m reminded of in this moment is that we, as an industry, have these platform shifts that unlock opportunities for companies who get lucky on timing. For example, the original dot-com era was really powered by Oracle and Sun Solaris boxes and data centers that you owned and operated yourself. We then went through a chapter where the infrastructure became Linux and open source for your data tier. Of course, we’ve had this huge long run of cloud infrastructure. I think that if you’re a company that builds your stack on Solaris and Oracle, it’s really that there’s an opportunity for a company to come along and build a stack on Linux and Postgres in that moment and suddenly find efficiencies that are very, very hard for you to claim. I think something very similar is happening in voice assistants. When I hear you talk on the show about your experience with voice assistants that are going through the transition from first generation to second generation, it feels to me like so much of the challenge there is about how we drag along all of the committed relationships that we have for the internet-connected toaster, back massager, and all of the things that are connected into those existing historical ecosystems. Honestly, even in the world of AI, with just how much has changed in the last couple of years underneath the companies as they’re building out their answers here, it really feels to me like we are stepping into a moment where agentic tool use powered by protocols, like MCP, is going to disintermediate a lot of that stuff that you’re talking about. I think that in the immediate term, we’re really excited about what we can do in the use cases that our customers are telling us they care about. Give me mood and audio in the home. We have great solutions for that today. And I think we can take advantage of this shift to a truly next-generation architecture without the baggage of a decade of internet-connected light switches from 17 different protocols with 17 different hubs in the closet. Well, I mean, part of the opportunity there is that you don’t have a big voice assistant. I don’t think the current Sonos voice assistant is at the scale of Alexa or Google Assistant. I’m just guessing. They do have that problem. The light switches in my house, they’re in the walls. They’re going to be there. That Lutron hub is there. It’s not great. However, Lutron is the best one. It is. It is the best one. There’s a box in my house, and there are a lot of those little weird little boxes in my house because I have a smart home, and all of those dependencies exist for those platforms for reasons. If you show up and say, “Use my voice assistant instead,” and it can’t operate all of the lights, well, I’m just going to fall back to Amazon, or I’m going to fall back to Google. They know it, and they know they can’t break those things. Panos and I have talked about it a lot, actually in the context of Alexa Plus. The promise of AI, at least from my very abstract vantage point, is, boy, I should not care about any of this. There’s a network in my house. There are lots of devices on that network. They have some access points on that network, and maybe they’re API-driven access points, maybe they’re MCP-driven. It should not matter. There’s just a bunch of devices in my network that you can control somehow, and this all-seeing robot that is going to replace every job in America should be able to traverse my network and turn on the lights without any help. That’s what it should do. Some of the very first big vibe coding shockwaves were AI researchers, bleeding-edge AI researchers, being like, “I figured out how to control my shades. They walked through my network, and the shades go up and down now,” right? We’re not there at the consumer level. The promise is not there. I’m still here talking to you about Matter, Thread, HomeKit, and whether or not Google Assistant can control my Sonos Amp, which, by the way, it can’t, and that is my one ticket to you that I didn’t submit on Threads. That’s the promise, but the gap to that seems really, really huge. Are you able to close it? Is that the opportunity? I think we’re just still in the Apple II days of the home automation space. So while there is, as you point out, this incredible, wild, heterogeneous world of different light switch controllers, I think when you talk to mainstream consumers about their homes, they’re not there yet. I do think that because of the profound technological step function of agentic control of these kinds of services and things like tool use, as the consumer catches up with the industry’s ambition to solve these problems, new technological solutions will emerge. I’m really excited about how we’re positioned to ride that transition and not be encumbered by the decade of early adopter internet-connected light switches. What are you going to do about the light switches that are already in the walls? I just don’t think that there’s enough of them to matter in the final answer. Of course, Lutron’s a great partner, and they do a great job with this. They do. I mean, we have them. We’ve got all kinds of light switches. We mostly have Lutron ones. But that’s my question. The first natural customer for something like what you’re describing is somebody who is already using these products in some way. If you show up to my house and there’s no Matter support or whatever, I’m like, “Well, I can’t use it.” Is it though, or is it more like the difference between the people that were adopting Creative Labs MP3 players before the iPod came along? Sure . Was the iPod really for those people, or was it for people that had that problem but were nowhere near the people that had been early adopters? Or was the iPhone for people that were using Windows CE, or was it for people that were using flip phones who were ready for the transition? I think we’re making- Is that the idea here “iPhone for smart home control” or “iPhone for audio in the home”? That’s right. The turn there that I think is really interesting is: who are you going to talk to? Where is the computer? What is the computer? You’re describing a situation where if you want music, you’re going to talk to Sonos. But you also have a general-purpose assistant like Claude or ChatGPT, and they can talk to Sonos, too. It’s unclear to me — and it may be one of the most fascinating questions at this moment in tech — where the interface goes. Are we all going to have one chatbot that does everything, and all the demand is aggregated there, and OpenAI becomes more powerful than ever? Or are we going to have lots and lots of assistants that we address in lots and lots of different ways? It seems like your bet is Sonos will have a personality in your home, maybe multiple personalities in your home, and customers will address that, and all the other stuff will go somewhere else. For 20 years, we’ve found a lot of success around the idea of embracing every dimension of the problem. Yes, there’s an app, but you’re welcome to engage with us through AirPlay or Spotify Connect. Yes, we have a voice assistant that lives side by side with Alexa. Yes, we have proprietary mesh, but it integrates with Bluetooth and even line-in. I think we bet that we’re of a size and scale that allows us to both be nimble and react to these changes, but also have enough horsepower to keep up technologically with what the best in the category are doing. So I think some of this just plays out on the field. Just one last idea, since you said it a couple of times, this question about where the compute lives. I think one incredibly powerful opportunity for Sonos is that we do place compute in millions and millions of homes. People don’t think of them as computers often, but they are. They create a seamless experience that is really the integration of a set of cloud services and local services in a way that looks like just one surface area to the customer. I think that the answer to your questions, “Does this live in the cloud? Does this live in the home? Does this live in a box?” is yes. I think we’re pretty uniquely situated to take advantage of an architecture where it’s not cloud-only, it’s not home-only, but it’s an integrated system that combines all of that together. And at the end of the day, that is what Sonos 27 is. Just to make that really reductive, when I say “where is the computer” in the home context, what I mean is maybe in the ’90s to early 2000s, there was a vision that we would all have home servers in our basements, and they would do all the logic of our home. They would have all the storage, and Microsoft would sell you a Windows home server in the basement and a Windows Media Center in the living room, and you and I probably both watched all of those Bill Gates keynotes at CES. None of that really ever came to pass. Instead, we put a lot of cheap computers near all the TVs, and they connected to cloud services, and they’re basically just running web browsers, as you well know. That is a very different version of what needed to happen and how the market played out. In the smart home, I’ve got a bunch of automations in my house. When the garage is open, the lights turn on, and other stuff happens. At night, the doors all lock if they’re not locked. That logic has to live somewhere. My perspective on it is that it should live in my house. If the internet goes down, the lights should still turn on. This is not anything to do with big AI integrations or the new MCP way to address the Sonos system. Those are big ideas, and I’m just insistently dragging you back down into the dirt of: if the internet goes out, are the lights still going to turn on? You don’t want to be the partner that puts in the internet-connected light switches that don’t work when the internet is down. But it’s not just the internet-connected light switches; it’s the logic of making it all work together. I understand. Yeah, fair. Here’s what I’ll say about that. For 40 years now, we’ve been talking about technology for the home, starting with the personal computer, which is supposed to be the center of the technological household, but we didn’t really get that. We got laptops that people mostly use at work and use a bit at home. Then we got mobile, and mobile is supposed to be the thing that you engage with when you leave your house on your way to work. Of course, the fundamental media of mobile is so addicting that it’s all-consuming. We use it at work, we use it at home — we use it all the time. But my observation about our use of it in the home is that nobody loves it. No spouse has ever said, “I wish my husband was on his phone more. I wish my kid used their iPad more,” and so we’re looking for ways to get beyond that. To your point, the other compute that’s in the home, like I said, is the set-top box, which is largely just a web browser to a bunch of services that live in the cloud. I think it’s pretty interesting, actually, that in 17 million homes Sonos is an actual mesh of compute in your house with real horsepower, real memory, real CPU, real capability, a real operating system — all just waiting to be the container for some of the kinds of things you’re talking about. So it’s super interesting. We’ll figure it out over time. I feel like you’re this close to being like, “And then the Teslas will be a data center.” There’s something there that is maybe the line. Actually, I want to talk about that. I actually want to push on that a little bit. The initial Sonos innovation 100 years ago, when the company started, was, “Oh, we can build a mesh network. We can do wireless audio at scale. We can synchronize the latency of all the speakers so it sounds like the same music playing at the same time.” This was a lot of big engineering back in the day. Still, I mean, candidly, still. A lot of what our software team does day in and day out is extend and maintain that infrastructure. There are features you’re announcing here as part of Sonos Fabric that I think are interesting. If you have surrounds, you can just place them, and they’ll figure out that they’re surrounds and immediately start being the surround speakers in a home theater. There’s just a lot of potential, as you’re describing, in the notion that, “Oh, there’s a big network of small computers in my house that can come together and do things you would not expect.” Is your focus that they will always do audio things? Or is it the focus that they will have many more capabilities? I think any thoughtful product leader is going to tell you the focus is an important part of success. I do feel like there’s so much interesting work for us to do around creating an audio system that sets the mood for your home that I don’t want us to take our eye off of that opportunity. We are doing some really exciting things in Sonos Fabric and Sonos 27 that we should talk about, that get to some of the work that you’re describing. But certainly in the moments where you allow yourself to think about what the company is in five years and what it will be in 10 years, you can’t help but interrogate what the opportunity is for a mesh — a fabric of compute that lives in the home. I want to end by talking about headphones really quickly. We just had the CEO of Bose on. She and I had a pretty searching conversation about what happens to the headphone market in the time of AI wearables. My fear, my anxiety, about audio is always that consumers will always pick convenience over quality. It’s just the history of the… I’ve got a set of AirPods on this desk, and they don’t sound great, but boy, are they convenient. And that’s just the way it goes. It has always been what the market has demanded: convenience over quality. We’re going to enter a time when Apple puts cameras on AirPods, and you can talk to them with Siri. When Google and Samsung ship very similar products, there’s undoubtedly going to be a flood of AI hardware startups that want to put something in your ears or in your body in some way. You are in the headphone market. You’re talking a lot about AI; you’re talking a lot about Fabric. That seems like a cataclysm coming for headphones. The same way that the removal of the headphone jack was a cataclysm in the headphone market, this seems like the next one. How are you preparing for that? Do you think there’s going to be a range of voice assistants on headphones, or do you think what you would call the first-party vendors are going to just grab more and more of that share? Before we jump to the hypotheticals about where headphones are, can I tell you a little bit about the new headphones? Yeah, of course. All right. So one of the things that you get from entering a new market is the opportunity to build something and put it in customers’ homes and learn a lot about what matters and what doesn’t matter. So we launched Sonos Ace two years ago. I think measured against any of the other premium over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones in the market, they’re a great product. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings. So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful. We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera. Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market. Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it. We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool. Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market. Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to. I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever. What do you think is going to happen? I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market. Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out? Sure. I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this. The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints. I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market. Yeah, sure. Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things. Super fun. Tell us what’s next for Sonos. When does all this stuff ship? So I think by the time this airs, we’ll have announced all of this to the world. We’re having a big event in New York to share Sonos OS 27, Sonos Voice 27, and the Ace Ultra and Beam Ultra. We can’t wait to get this stuff out into the world and begin to hear what our customers do with all of these exciting new products. Many of the software features are going to be available in early access, which will mean our customers will opt into them, be able to give us feedback, and we’ll be able to observe the telemetry that comes back from their homes and make sure that we’re delivering exactly the experience that we want. We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us. As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond. That’s great. All right, I’ve got to ask you at the end: I have ceiling speakers in my kitchen. They’re connected to a Sonos Amp. There’s a Google Home Hub right there, and it’s broken. I can’t ask it to play music in the kitchen. When are you going to fix that for me? I’m ending on tech support. All right. I don’t know the answer, but I’d love to figure it out for you. I know the right folks to call, so let’s get you connected. We’re going to have a Decoder roundtable. If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily. Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan. All right. Right on. Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man. This was super fun. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand.

Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 .

I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.

Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system.

There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices.

article.title: Microsoft Defender is falsely flagging Google links as malicious
article.summary: Even though Microsoft Defender is more than enough security on its own , its reputation has taken a bit of a hit this year. Over the last few months, vulnerabilities like RedSun and RoguePlanet were discovered (and later patched), while just last month Defender was showing false warnings that it was disabled even when it wasn’t .

Over the last few months, vulnerabilities like RedSun and RoguePlanet were discovered (and later patched), while just last month Defender was showing false warnings that it was disabled even when it wasn’t .

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: The latest Defender issue to crop up is that it’s now incorrectly classifying Google links as malicious, reports Neowin . Specifically affecting Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and confirmed by Microsoft, this bug shows an “Opening this website might not be safe” warning when trying to open legitimate Google links.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: Microsoft says it has identified the cause of the issue, clarifying that it isn’t an actual security threat with Google links:.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links may block the opening of Google search links (URLs), identifying them as malicious. In addition, admins may receive related alerts and incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal and Microsoft Sentinel as a result of these detections. We’ve determined that an inaccurate security classification is causing legitimate Google search URLs to be incorrectly identified as malicious, resulting in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links blocking access to affected links. We’re working to correct the misclassification to remediate impact.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: Microsoft says it’s working on a fix, but hasn’t given a specific timeline regarding when the fix will be released.

Pixel Watch owners can now add Air quality index, Pollen, and Precipitation complications to their watch face. Some third-party Wear OS weather apps already offer some of these complications for Pixel Watch owners.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: Google retired the existing Weather app for Pixel Watch models last year in favor of the Pixel Weather app . Since then, the app has allowed Pixel Watch owners to choose from up to three watch face complications: Sunrise and sunset, UV Index, and Weather. Now, a new Pixel Weather update for Wear OS is adding three more complications to the list.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: Google is rolling out dedicated complications for Air quality index, Pollen, and Precipitation as part of the version 1.0.0.94 update of the Pixel Weather app. For the uninitiated, complications on smartwatches are like widgets that offer information in real time on the watch face. draft_context.source_title: Drowning in CVEs and thirsty for answers? Try CTEM
draft_context.description: A decade or two ago, board executives asked "why should I care about cybersecurity?" Five years ago, they were asking "Are you patching our software vulnerabilities?" Now, they're starting to ask: "Are we actually secure?" They might want a simple 'yes' or 'no' initially, but eventually they'll say the most dreaded thing of all, and it'll be a demand, not a question: "Prove it". Traditional vulnerability management and patching, won't survive that conversation. It's why a relatively new approach is gaining traction: Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM). What's wrong with vulnerability management We define security flaws using Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), and we tell each other how bad they are by assigning the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) to them. There are three problems with that. There's a firehose of CVEs, the CVSS scores aren't helpful when triaging them, and AI is about to make the whole thing much worse. CISOs are drowning in CVEs. The industry has spent decades creating tools that churn out vulnerability data and others that consume it. Few if any tell you which vulnerabilities an attacker could use to hurt you in your environment. The volume of CVEs is making traditional vulnerability management (patch it and forget it) less tractable every year, says Drew Vanover, principal security strategist at Horizon3. "Think about the last patch release that Microsoft put out," he says. "There were over 500 fixes in one patch cycle. That is incomprehensible. Nobody is going to be able to go through, vet, prioritize, and deploy all of those in a way that is truly considered safe." The number of CVEs created each year has been soaring, putting more pressure on the US’ National Institute for Standards and Technology's National Vulnerability Database, which has now been backlogged for years. NIST threw up its hands in April and effectively declared CVE bankruptcy. The US Department of Commerce highlighted the second issue (that current severity metrics aren't useful) as part of a report this May. Aside from launching a zinger at the NIST by saying that the NVD was poorly managed, it also suggested that it stop assigning CVSS scores altogether. These are highly subjective, it said. They also depend on exactly what the exposed system is doing in a particular organization's infrastructure. Is a critical severity score in a product important if only one sandboxed system ever interacts with it? Or could an attacker chain three apparently innocuous vulns to cause damage that a business executive would care about? AI will make vulnerability management harder These complex problems are a headache, but AI is about to turn it into a full-on migraine. Frontier LLMs like Claude's Mythos are already surfacing zero-days at scale, heralding a flood of CVEs. They don't just find bugs at scale; they also work much more quickly than their human counterparts to create and weaponize exploits. This makes it even more important that organizations patch the right bugs quickly. The Cloud Security Alliance now describes an asymmetric vulnerability cycle in which attackers can use AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities more quickly, (increasingly before patches are even released), while organizations are taking longer to patch them. What is CTEM? Something has to change. Gartner figured this out in 2023, when it named CTEM a top cybersecurity trend. This is a way of staying on top of your vulnerabilities by triaging them properly. To do that, you have to go beyond the technical implications of a security flaw and understand what it really means for your business. Gartner lays out five steps to CTEM: ● Scoping Find the assets that carry significant business impact and prioritize them. ● Discovery Find how they're exposed by analyzing their weaknesses in depth. ● Prioritization Rank those exposures based on real business risk. ● Validation Test out the vulnerabilities to see if they're exploitable. ● Mobilization Fix them with a proper incident response plan. How automated pen testing helps manage vulnerabilities This approach promises to nail the security flaws that matter to an organization, but it's also more complex than traditional vulnerability management. It needs automation, which is what Horizon3 is providing with NodeZero. Scoping out systems is a commodity practice these days. So is discovery. Horizon3 is leaving those to partners so it can focus on the parts of the CTEM framework that aren't yet easy for customers to solve. Those are prioritization by business impact, and mobilization. NodeZero runs penetration tests across an organization's infrastructure and documents the exploitable paths with evidence a defender can follow. The output is the wheat sifted from the chaff; a shorter list of exposures that security teams and developers can focus on. The impressive part here is the chain-of-attack behavior. NodeZero probes for weaknesses, exploits them, and then pivots based on what it finds. This means it adapts to the environment to extend its attack, just as a real attacker adapts attacks and moves laterally through systems. This approach is based on a deterministic machine learning expert system rather than a general LLM, explains Vanover. "A good analogy is to think about the medical profession," he says. "A GP is your general LLM trying to cover everything. They know a little bit about a lot, but they aren't the experts, and that's where you start having hallucinations and guesses and misses." The company only uses generative AI for specific tasks. Using it to parse a two petabyte S3 blob looking for sensitive data or identifying high-value credentials, with data staying inside the customer's boundary via AWS Bedrock, for example. What it doesn't do is run amok spawning rogue agents in your system. Vanover says the value here is in proving that you've clobbered load-bearing security bugs. "If we say that we can exploit something, it's because we did, and we'll show you the proof in the platform," he says. The next step is closing the loop by retesting the exploit after it's been dealt with. Teams get to close tickets because NodeZero can no longer traverse the attack path. That is a testable definition of "fixed" and one that translates into a risk metric a CFO can read. Horizon3 also wants to solve customers' tool sprawl problems with a single product that handles all of the heavy CTEM lifting. A common failure mode of enterprise CTEM programs is a stack of vendors whose handoffs create precisely the blind spots the framework was meant to eliminate. That disappears when it's all under one service. Is automated penetration testing safe? CISOs might be nervous letting an autonomous penetration testing system loose on production systems. It sounds like something that could break running processes. Why not just test against a digital twin instead? Testing in production is the safest way to find bugs, retorts Vanover. That's because environments drift frequently, especially in an agile world driven by short development sprints and automated changes to code. If a user changes a password or a team pushes a feature fragment, a digital twin system won't reflect reality. So Horizon3 focuses on strong production guardrails instead. "I don't need to ransom your system to prove to you that I can ransom it," Vanover says. "If I can get on the system, install a remote access tool, create a file, encrypt the file, and delete that file, I've just proven that I can ransom your system." He says Horizon3 has run more than 320,000 production tests across customer organizations. These include some that are especially nervous about what's poking around in their systems, such as the NSA and the largest medical records processor on the planet, along with a couple of large healthcare providers. Where can I start with CTEM? Gartner's CTEM framework is powerful, but it might also be daunting for CISOs. Vanover advises them to begin by picking one thing and doing it well. "No organization is going to implement CTEM in a year. That is a recipe for failure," he says. "Break it down. Look at places for the low-hanging fruit." You could do worse than look at what systems are actually reachable instead of blindly trusting an asset inventory that might be out of date. The race is on to embrace CTEM, because metrics like the number of patches applied won't satisfy the board for much longer. They don't describe how much exploitable surface still exists. The point of running the CTEM loop is to move reporting from activity to outcomes, so that the board gets to see fewer exploitable paths and a smaller blast radius. The new goal is to prove that a security control worked, not just that you paid for it. Want to operationalize CTEM but don’t know where to start? Check out this whitepaper from Horizon3

article.title: If your old Chromecast and Google Home devices are having setup issues, you’re not alone — thankfully, Google’s latest update has fixed this
article.summary: These issues first arose when Google announced it would be ending support for its oldest Chromecast dongles back in May. From there, owners started reporting problems with setting up their devices after they started disappearing from the Google Home app on Android.
article.dek: These issues first arose when Google announced it would be ending support for its oldest Chromecast dongles back in May.
article.hook: These issues first arose when Google announced it would be ending support for its oldest Chromecast dongles back in May.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: These issues first arose when Google announced it would be ending support for its oldest Chromecast dongles back in May. From there, owners started reporting problems with setting up their devices after they started disappearing from the Google Home app on Android.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: A Google Home app update made setting up Chromecast even more difficult which, understandably, sparked a lot of worry for those who are still using the first-gen Chromecast from over 10 years ago, convincing them that Google was officially pulling the plug on its OG streaming device. Similar issues then started cropping up for owners of the 2015 Chromecast model and Google Home Mini speaker, affecting functionality as well as the setup process.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: At first, users were left to find their own workarounds and solutions, with many having to factory reset their devices, revert to older versions of the Google Home app, or even wipe their entire Home ecosystem to start afresh. Thankfully, Google has solved this, implying that these setup and functionality crashes were part of a software glitch.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: The Google Nest Community account on Reddit replied to a series of frustrated posts with the following statement: ‘We've resolved an issue that was impacting the ability to set up some older Chromecast and Google Home devices. If you haven't already, factory reset your speaker or update your Google Home app to version 4.26 and try again’.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: Google Home update adds new Gemini voice commands and Spotify fixes Google is working on fix for Home Speaker voice assistant delays Google Home Speakers now support wireless pairing with Google TV Streamer It hasn’t been the best time to be a first-gen Chromecast owner to say the least, but at least Google’s latest fix offers some reassurance that the company isn’t writing off its oldest streaming device yet — despite pulling the first Chromecast from shelves in early 2025 . That said, Google isn’t the first tech giant to be accused of intentionally bricking older streaming devices to get users to upgrade.

A Google Home app update made setting up Chromecast even more difficult which, understandably, sparked a lot of worry for those who are still using the first-gen Chromecast from over 10 years ago, convincing them that Google was officially pulling the plug on its OG streaming device. Similar issues then started cropping up for owners of the 2015 Chromecast model and Google Home Mini speaker, affecting functionality as well as the setup process.

At first, users were left to find their own workarounds and solutions, with many having to factory reset their devices, revert to older versions of the Google Home app, or even wipe their entire Home ecosystem to start afresh. Thankfully, Google has solved this, implying that these setup and functionality crashes were part of a software glitch.

The Google Nest Community account on Reddit replied to a series of frustrated posts with the following statement: ‘We've resolved an issue that was impacting the ability to set up some older Chromecast and Google Home devices. If you haven't already, factory reset your speaker or update your Google Home app to version 4.26 and try again’.

Amazon received similar backlash when a user filed a lawsuit against the company , after reporting that two Fire TV sticks ran into severe performance issues just a few years after purchasing them. The user claimed that Amazon had been software tethering, while not disclosing the truth about the lifespan of its Fire TV stick streamers.
